lesson_title: One Sentence, Two Lists, Three Sketches
hook_text: Every design in the world starts the same way: one sentence, two lists, three rough sketches.
clip_script: Here is how a design begins. Step one, one sentence. Who needs it, what they need, what kind of thing will do it, where. Design and make a hand-operated lifting device in a stable frame so one adult can raise a water container onto a stand. Notice: no gears, no pulleys. The sentence is the problem, not the answer. Step two, two lists. Musts: it must lift the load, hold it at the top, not topple, keep fingers away from the gears. Limits: this big, these materials, two lessons, this budget. Make every must testable. Step three, three sketches. Rough, pencil, no ruler, labels and arrows, and genuinely different: a pulley, a gear, a lever. Then a table: ideas across, musts and limits down, tick, tick, cross. The most ticks wins, and you write why. One sentence, two lists, three sketches. Now you are designing.
visual_style: Whiteboard builds a single sentence word by word, then two columns of short lines, then three quick thumbnail sketches that get labels and arrows, then a tick table.
pacing: Three steps of about eighteen seconds each, closing on the tick table.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and write your own one-sentence brief for the PAT scenario.
